package.description:

package.pinned_comment: Measure yourself tonight and tomorrow morning: how much taller were you? 📏
package.script: You lose one centimeter of height every day, but why? Your spine isn't one solid bone. It's a stack of vertebrae, with twenty-three squishy discs in between. Each disc is like a jelly doughnut, with a soft, watery middle. All day, gravity pushes down on you. Every step and every sit squeezes a little water out, and the discs flatten a tiny bit. Add up all twenty-three, and you've shrunk about a centimeter by bedtime. But when you lie down to sleep, the weight comes off your spine. The discs soak water back up, like little sponges, and by morning, you're tall again. In space, with no gravity, astronauts can grow three percent taller! So tonight, measure yourself before bed, then again when you wake up. Will you be one centimeter taller tomorrow morning?
key_facts: The intervertebral discs between vertebrae compress under load during the day, so people are typically around 1 cm (often quoted up to about 2 cm) shorter by evening (scienceblog; mechse.illinois.edu)
The adult spine has 23 intervertebral discs, each with a tough outer ring (annulus fibrosus) and a soft, water-rich gel centre (nucleus pulposus)
Lying down removes the load and the discs rehydrate overnight, restoring height by morning
Without gravity, astronauts' spines lengthen and they can grow up to about 3% taller in space (Scientific American; Space.com)

package.pinned_comment: Which trick would you pick to survive the winter: sugar, supercooling, antifreeze, or drying out?
package.script: Frozen solid for seven months. No heartbeat. No breathing. You'd be dead. This frog just hops away in spring. So how do animals survive being frozen? Today, four champions of the cold, each with a totally different trick. Meet the wood frog. It lives as far north as Alaska, and it doesn't hide from winter. It just lies down under the leaves, and lets the ice come. The problem with freezing is sharp ice crystals. If they grow inside a cell, they rip it apart like tiny knives. So the frog plays a clever game. As ice touches its skin, its liver floods the body with sugar, up to ten times the normal amount. That sugar soaks into every cell, like a syrup that won't freeze. So the ice can only grow outside the cells, in the spaces in between. Up to sixty percent of the frog turns to ice. No heartbeat. No breath. In Alaska, it can stay like this for as long as seven months. Then spring comes, the ice melts, and the heart starts beating again. Our second champion uses the opposite trick. The Arctic ground squirrel never freezes at all, even when its body drops below zero. Scientists measured one at almost minus three degrees, the coldest body ever found in a mammal. How? It's called supercooling. Water needs a tiny seed to start freezing, like a speck of dust, or a bit of ice. The squirrel's blood is so clean, there's nothing for ice to grow on. So it stays liquid, below freezing. But that's risky. So every few weeks, the squirrel shivers, warms itself back up for a little while, then drops back into the deep cold. Now, dive under the Antarctic ice. The sea here is almost minus two degrees, cold enough to freeze most fish solid. But these Antarctic fish swim around just fine. Their blood is full of antifreeze proteins. When a tiny ice crystal sneaks in, the proteins grab onto it, and wrap it up so it can't grow. One of their cousins, the icefish, went even further. Its blood has no red cells at all. It's clear, like water. And then there's the toughest of them all. The tardigrade, or water bear, smaller than a grain of sand. When things get bad, it dries itself out, curls into a tiny ball called a tun, and basically pauses its life. In nineteen eighty three, scientists collected moss in Antarctica, and kept it in a freezer at minus twenty. Thirty years later, they thawed it out. Two water bears woke up, and one of them went on to lay nineteen eggs. So why do scientists care? Because we can't do this yet. A donor heart on ice only lasts about four to six hours. Researchers are studying the frog's sugar, and the fish's antifreeze, to keep organs alive for much longer. Four animals, four tricks: sugar, supercooling, antifreeze, and drying out. Which one would you pick? Next time, how did a bitter bean become the world's favorite treat, chocolate?
key_facts: Wood frogs: up to ~60% of the body freezes, heart and breathing stop, glucose up to ~10x normal acts as a cryoprotectant; in Alaska up to ~7 months frozen (Audubon)
Arctic ground squirrel: supercools to about -2.9 C, lowest body temperature recorded in a mammal; rewarms every few weeks (UAF)
Antarctic notothenioid fish: seawater about -1.9 C, antifreeze glycoproteins bind ice crystals; icefish have no red blood cells / hemoglobin, colorless blood (Wikipedia: Antarctic fishes)
Tardigrades: moss collected in Antarctica Nov 1983, stored at -20 C, thawed 2014; two revived, one laid 19 eggs (phys.org 2016)
Donor hearts are typically kept on ice for about 4-6 hours

package.title: Why Can't You Tickle Yourself? 0.2 Seconds Changes It 🤔
package.description:
Why can't you tickle yourself? Your cerebellum predicts the touch from your own movement and turns the feeling down, but in a robot experiment, adding a delay of just 0.2 seconds made self-tickling feel more ticklish.

package.pinned_comment: Have you EVER managed to tickle yourself? Tell me how 👇
package.script: Your brain cancels your own tickles before you feel them. But how? Every time you move, your brain sends a copy of the order to the cerebellum, at the back of your head. It predicts what the touch will feel like, then turns the feeling down. No surprise, no tickle. When someone else tickles you, there's no prediction. Your brain can't guess where or when, so it hits full blast. Scientists tested this with a robot. People moved a handle, and a robot brushed their palm. Moving it themselves? Barely ticklish. Then the robot added a delay of just two tenths of a second. Suddenly, it felt more ticklish. The prediction was off, so the brain couldn't cancel it. So your own brain blocks the tickle. Can you find a way to outsmart it?
key_facts: Every movement sends a copy of the motor command to the cerebellum, which predicts the sensory result and dampens it (Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith).
Touch from someone else can't be predicted, so it isn't dampened.
In a robot-arm experiment, delaying the self-produced touch by 0.2 seconds made it feel more ticklish.

package.title: Your Fridge Stales Bread 6x Faster 🍞
package.description:
Why does bread go stale, and why is it faster in the fridge? Stale bread isn't mostly dried out: as it cools, its starch slowly packs back into crystals (retrogradation) that squeeze out and lock away water, and that happens fastest just above freezing, so the fridge can stale bread up to about six times faster, while the freezer almost stops it and warming re-melts the crystals for a while.

package.pinned_comment: Fridge, counter or freezer: where does YOUR bread live? 🍞
package.script: Your fridge is wasting your bread. It can go stale six times faster. But why? Fresh bread is soft because of starch. In the oven, starch soaks up water, and its tight crystals melt into a soft gel. But once the bread cools, the starch packs back into crystals. Scientists call it retrogradation. Those crystals squeeze the water out, and lock it away. So the crumb turns hard, even though it's barely dried out. That's why sealed bread still goes stale. And this crystal building runs fastest just above freezing, right at fridge temperature. In the freezer, it almost stops. The fix? Warm stale bread in the oven, and the crystals melt again. It goes soft, almost like fresh, but only for a little while. So, fridge, counter, or freezer: where does your bread live?

package.title: Why Don't Woodpeckers Get Headaches? 🐦
package.description:
Woodpeckers hammer trees up to 20 times a second at over 1,000 g, so why don't woodpeckers get brain damage or headaches? A 2022 slow-motion study found the skull is a stiff hammer, not a shock absorber, and their tiny brains can handle far bigger hits than ours.

package.pinned_comment: What would YOU headbang 20 times a second? 🐦
package.script: Woodpeckers headbang trees twenty times a second, and you'd be out cold after one. So why don't they get headaches? Each peck stops the head in about a thousandth of a second. That's over a thousand g. For years, people thought the skull was a spongy crash helmet. But in 2022, slow-motion videos showed it barely cushions anything. It's a stiff hammer, because a soft one would hit weaker. The real trick is size. A woodpecker's brain weighs just a few grams, packed so snugly it barely sloshes. Tiny brains handle far bigger hits than ours. Plus, its long tongue bone wraps all the way around its skull, which may help keep things steady. That's up to twelve thousand pecks a day, and not one headache. So what would you headbang twenty times a second?

A woodpecker brain weighs only a few grams and fits snugly, and small brains tolerate much higher decelerations

package.description:
Why do cut apples turn brown? Slicing an apple bursts its cells, so the enzyme polyphenol oxidase meets the apple's polyphenols and oxygen, turning them into brown pigment, and lemon juice slows it down.

package.script:
Why does your apple grow a brown scab in 5 minutes?
Inside every apple cell,
two things are locked in separate rooms.
One holds an enzyme, polyphenol oxidase.
The other holds natural chemicals called polyphenols.
When you bite or slice the apple,
you burst thousands of cells.
The two finally meet,
and oxygen from the air rushes in.
The enzyme uses that oxygen
to turn the polyphenols into brown pigment,
like the melanin in your skin.
Scientists think it's a defence,
a brown shield against germs and bugs,
just like a scab on your knee.
Want to stop it?
Squeeze on some lemon juice.
Its acid slows the enzyme down,
and its vitamin C grabs the oxygen first.
So when your apple turns brown,
is it rotting, or healing?
Tell me in the comments.
key_facts: Cutting or biting bursts apple cells, letting the enzyme polyphenol oxidase (PPO) meet the apple's polyphenols, which are stored in a separate compartment
With oxygen from the air, PPO turns polyphenols into quinones that link into brown melanin-like pigments
Browning starts within minutes of cutting
Scientists think the browning helps protect the fruit against microbes and insects
Lemon juice slows browning: its acid slows the enzyme and its vitamin C (ascorbic acid) acts as an antioxidant

package.title: How Chocolate Went From 5,300-Year-Old Bean to Bar
package.description:
The history of chocolate, from cacao beans used 5,300 years ago in the Amazon and the Maya's bitter foamy drink, to Aztec cocoa-bean money, the first chocolate bar in 1847 and the invention of milk chocolate. Plus why chocolate melts in your mouth but not in your hand.

Sources:

https://popular-archaeology.com/article/the-indians-of-the-ecuadorian-amazon-were-using-cocoa-5300-years-ago/
https://cocoarunners.com/2022/07/an-industrial-history-of-chocolate/

package.pinned_comment: Would you rather have the old spicy chocolate drink or a modern bar? 🍫
package.script: You could buy a turkey with a hundred cocoa beans. So why did chocolate stop being money, and how did it end up in your hand? This is the story of chocolate. It starts with a tree in the rainforest. The cacao tree grows big, football-shaped pods, right on its trunk. Inside each pod are thirty to fifty seeds, wrapped in sweet white pulp. Those seeds are cocoa beans. Scientists found traces of cacao in pots from the Amazon in Ecuador, about five thousand three hundred years old. Later, the Olmec and the Maya turned the beans into a drink. They roasted them, ground them into paste, and mixed in water, chili, and cornmeal. Then they poured it from high up, from one cup into another, to whip up a thick foam on top. And here's the thing. It wasn't sweet at all. It was bitter, spicy, and very special. The Aztecs loved it so much they used the beans as money. One record from the fifteen hundreds lists prices. A tomato cost one bean. An avocado, three beans. A turkey hen, one hundred. Some people even made fake beans, by stuffing empty shells with mud. Then, in the fifteen hundreds, Spanish explorers carried cacao back across the ocean. The Spanish court tried the bitter drink, and did something new. They added sugar, plus cinnamon and vanilla. Suddenly, Europe was hooked. Fancy chocolate houses opened in London, where rich people sipped it hot. But for almost three hundred years, chocolate was still only a drink. Here's why. A cocoa bean is about half fat, called cocoa butter. Grind the beans, and you get a thick, greasy paste. In eighteen twenty eight, a Dutch chemist named Coenraad van Houten built a press that squeezed out most of that butter. What was left became a dry cake, that could be crushed into cocoa powder. Then in eighteen forty seven, an English company called Fry's flipped the idea. They mixed cocoa powder and sugar with extra melted cocoa butter, and poured it into a mold. It set hard. The first modern chocolate bar. It was still gritty, and a bit bitter. Two Swiss makers fixed that. In eighteen seventy five, Daniel Peter added milk, using milk powder from his neighbor, Henri Nestlé. Milk chocolate was born. Then in eighteen seventy nine, Rodolphe Lindt built a machine called a conche. It rolls warm chocolate back and forth for hours, grinding every bit smaller and smaller, until it turns silky smooth. So what happens today? Farmers cut open the pods and let the beans ferment for about a week. That's where most of the chocolate flavor comes from. Then the beans are dried, roasted, and cracked. It takes around four hundred beans to make one pound of chocolate. And the best trick is in the butter. Cocoa butter melts at about thirty four degrees Celsius, just below the heat inside your mouth. That's why a bar stays solid in your hand, but melts on your tongue. From a bitter drink worth real money, to the bar in your lunchbox. So, would you rather have the drink, or the bar? Next time, how do tiny ants build an underground city for millions of workers?
key_facts: Traces of cacao in ~5,300-year-old pottery from the Ecuadorian Amazon (2018 study)
Olmec and Maya drank cacao as a bitter, foamy drink with chili and cornmeal
Aztecs used cacao beans as money; a 1545 list: tomato 1 bean, avocado 3, turkey hen 100
Spanish added sugar, cinnamon and vanilla; London chocolate houses from 1657
1828 van Houten press separates cocoa butter; 1847 Fry's first solid bar
1875 Daniel Peter milk chocolate with Nestle's milk; 1879 Lindt's conche
~400 beans per pound of chocolate; cocoa butter melts ~34 C, below mouth temperature

topic.title: Why do we get goosebumps?

package.title: Why Do We Get Goosebumps? 🥶
package.description:
Why do we get goosebumps? Tiny arrector pili muscles at almost every hair squeeze when you're cold or scared, pulling the hair upright and raising a bump of skin, a leftover from furry ancestors whose fluffed-up fur trapped warm air and made them look bigger.

Sources:
https://www.livescience.com/32349-what-causes-goose-bumps.html
https://hscrb.harvard.edu/news/the-real-reason-behind-goosebumps
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499948/

Animated in the Chalkboard Lesson style.

package.pinned_comment: What gives you goosebumps every single time: a song, a scary movie, or cold air?
package.script:
Your skin hides five million tiny muscles. Why?
Almost every hair on your body
has its own muscle,
called the arrector pili.
When you get cold,
or scared,
your nerves fire one signal,
and they all squeeze at once.
That yanks each hair upright,
and pushes up a bump of skin.
That's a goosebump.
For a furry animal, it's a superpower.
Standing fur traps a layer of warm air,
like a puffy winter coat.
And a scared cat puffs up,
so it looks bigger.
But we lost most of our fur,
so now we just get bumps.
Even a song can trigger them,
because big feelings fire the same nerves.
And in mice, scientists found
those nerves wake up hair stem cells,
to grow thicker fur in the cold.
So what gives you goosebumps?
key_facts: The body has about 5 million hair follicles, and almost every body hair has a tiny arrector pili muscle attached
Cold or fear triggers the sympathetic nervous system, which makes the arrector pili muscles contract
The contraction pulls the hair upright and raises a small bump of skin: a goosebump
In furry mammals, raised fur traps a layer of insulating air and makes the animal look bigger to threats
Strong emotions, such as from music, can trigger the same nervous response
A 2020 Harvard study in mice found the sympathetic nerves tied to these muscles also activate hair follicle stem cells to grow new hair in prolonged cold

topic.title: Why don't flamingos fall over standing on one leg?

package.title: Why Don't Flamingos Fall Over? 🦩
package.description:
Why don't flamingos fall over standing on one leg? A 2017 study found a flamingo's body weight locks its leg joints in place, so standing on one leg takes almost no muscle effort; even a dead flamingo balanced on one leg but not on two.

Sources:
https://news.emory.edu/stories/2017/05/ting_flamingoes/index.html
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/study-explores-how-flamingos-stay-stable-one-leg-180963440/
https://theconversation.com/scientists-balanced-a-dead-flamingo-on-one-leg-to-unlock-the-birds-standing-secret-78231

package.pinned_comment: How many seconds can you stand on one leg with your eyes closed?
package.script:
A dead flamingo can stand on one leg.
Why can't you?
In 2017, scientists in Atlanta tested it.
They propped up a flamingo body,
and it balanced on one leg,
with no muscles working at all.
Here's the trick.
That bendy joint isn't a knee.
It's the ankle.
The real knee is hidden up in the feathers.
When a flamingo lifts one leg,
it shifts its body,
so its weight sits right over the foot.
That weight pushes the joints into a locked position,
like a folding chair clicking open.
No muscles needed, just gravity.
Live flamingos even sway less
when they're fast asleep.
But on two legs,
the dead bird couldn't stay up.
For a flamingo, one leg is the lazy way to stand.
For you, it's a muscle workout.
So how long can you stand on one leg?
key_facts: In a 2017 Biology Letters study (Georgia Tech and Emory, Atlanta), a flamingo cadaver could be posed stably on one leg with no muscle activity, a 'passive gravitational stay mechanism'
The same cadaver could not stand stably on two legs
The backward-bending joint seen mid-leg is the ankle; the knee is hidden up in the body feathers
On one leg the bird shifts so its centre of mass sits over the foot, and body weight holds the joints in a locked position
Live juvenile flamingos swayed less when resting or asleep on one leg than when awake

topic.title: Why does your stomach growl?

package.title: Why Your Stomach Growls Every 2 Hours
package.description:
Why does your stomach growl, and why is it loudest when it's empty? Your gut is a muscle tube that squeezes food, liquid and gas along in waves (peristalsis); when it's empty there's nothing to muffle the sound, and every one to two hours a cleaning wave sweeps leftovers and bacteria down the gut, rumbling for 10 to 20 minutes until you eat.

Sources:
https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/why-does-your-stomach-gro/
https://www.livescience.com/health/food-diet/why-do-our-stomachs-growl

package.pinned_comment: When did your stomach growl at the WORST possible moment? Exam, meeting, silent library?
package.script: Your empty stomach growls every two hours until you eat. But why won't it stop? Your gut is one long muscle tube, and its walls squeeze in waves. That's called peristalsis. They push food, liquid and gas along, about three squeezes a minute in your stomach. After a meal, food muffles the sound. But empty? It's mostly gas and air, so every squeeze echoes like a drum. When you've been empty a while, a big cleaning wave kicks in. It sweeps leftover food and bacteria down the whole gut. It rumbles for ten to twenty minutes, then comes back every one to two hours, until you eat again. The ancient Greeks called it borborygmi, which means rumbling. So that growl isn't just hunger. It's your gut taking out the trash. When did your stomach growl at the worst moment?
key_facts: Stomach and gut noises are called borborygmi, an ancient Greek word that means rumbling (Scientific American).

Peristalsis: wave-like muscle contractions push food, liquid and gas through the stomach and small intestine; the basic rhythm is about 3 waves a minute in the stomach (Scientific American, Live Science).
Growling is louder when the stomach and intestines are empty because there's no food to muffle it; the tract is mostly gas and air (both sources).

After about two hours empty, cleaning waves (migrating motor complexes) start, last 10-20 minutes, and repeat every one to two hours until you eat, sweeping leftover food, mucus and bacteria along (Scientific American).
It can happen on an empty or a full stomach (both sources).

topic.title: Why do cats' eyes glow in the dark?

package.title: Why Do Cats' Eyes Glow? They Need 1/6 the Light You Do 🐱
package.description:
Why do cats' eyes glow in the dark? They don't make light: a mirror-like layer behind the retina, the tapetum lucidum, bounces light back through the eye for a second chance, which helps cats see in about one-sixth of the light humans need.

Sources:

https://www.catster.com/lifestyle/why-do-cat-eyes-glow-in-the-dark

package.pinned_comment: What color do your cat's eyes shine at night: green, yellow, or something else? 👇
package.script: Cat eyes never glow, that shine is your own flashlight bouncing back at you. Light comes in through the pupil, and hits the retina at the back of the eye. Tiny cells catch it, and send a picture to the brain. But in your eye, some light slips right past them, and it's gone. A cat gets a second chance. Behind its retina sits a shiny layer, called the tapetum lucidum. It works like a mirror, bouncing missed light back through the retina. So a cat needs just one-sixth of the light you do. Whatever still isn't caught, shoots back out of the eye. That's the shine, often green or yellow. No light at all? No shine, and no sight either. Ever caught your cat's eyes shining at night? What color were they?
key_facts: Cat eyes reflect light rather than making it; the tapetum lucidum sits behind the retina and bounces light back for a second chance (NPR, Catster).
Cats need about one-sixth of the light humans need to see (Purina, MetLife).
Cats often shine green, Siamese cats often yellow; riboflavin or zinc in the tapetum and retinal pigment affect the colour (NPR).
Cats cannot see when absolutely all light is blocked (Purina, MetLife).

package.script: Your cat's purr is a twitch, twenty-five times a second. But how? Deep in the throat sits the voice box, with a tiny gap called the glottis. A signal from the brain makes the muscles around it twitch, snapping that gap open and shut. Air rushes in, and the gap chops it into bursts. Air flows out, and it chops it again. Bobcats and cheetahs purr too, but lions and tigers don't seem to. And a purr doesn't always mean happy. Cats also purr at the vet, or when they're hurt. So when yours starts twitching away, do you think it's happy, or worried?

package.title: How Do Ants Run a City With 7,000 Rooms?
package.description:
What happens inside a leafcutter ant colony? Follow the leaves underground into a city of millions, with fungus farms, bodyguard ants, garbage rooms, wind-powered chimneys and one queen who started it all.

Sources:

package.pinned_comment: Which job would you pick in the ant city: leaf hauler, bodyguard, fungus gardener, or trash duty?
package.script: Ants built farms fifty million years before you, and you'd never spot them. And right now, under a rainforest floor, there's an ant city with millions of citizens, thousands of rooms, farms, garbage dumps, and its own air conditioning. So what actually happens inside a leafcutter ant city? It starts up here, on the road. Leafcutter ants march along forest trails in long green parades. Each worker slices off a piece of leaf with her jaws, then hauls it home, carrying up to ten times her own weight. That's like you jogging home with a cow on your back. But look closer. There's a tiny ant riding on top of that leaf. She's the bodyguard. Tiny flies try to lay eggs in the carriers' heads, so this little passenger fends them off. Because in this city, everybody has a job, and your size is your job description. The tiniest ants, called minims, have heads less than a millimeter wide. They look after the babies and the gardens. Medium ants are the foragers you just met. And the giants are the soldiers, with heads up to seven millimeters wide. Now, follow the leaves underground. Here's the twist. They don't really eat them. They'll sip a little sap, but the leaf is just fertilizer. Smaller ants snip each piece into tiny bits. Gardeners crush those bits into pellets, add a drop of their own poop, and press it all into a giant spongy garden. What grows there is a fungus. That's the real food. It feeds babies and adults, and they've been passing this crop down for millions of years. But every farmer has a weed problem. A rival fungus can wreck the whole crop. So the ants wear a white powder on their bodies. That powder is bacteria, and it makes antibiotics that hold the weed back. Infected patches get chopped out and dragged away, which brings us to the trash. Waste goes to separate garbage rooms, some big enough for you to stand inside. The workers there are mostly older ants, kept apart from everyone else. A city this big has one more problem. Breathing. All that fungus and all those ants make carbon dioxide. The ants can handle it. Their fungus can't. So one species builds chimneys. When wind blows across the mound, it pulls stale air out of the top holes, and fresh air gets drawn in. Those turrets can boost the airflow up to ten times. No fans. No electricity. So who started all this? The queen. She can live up to fifteen years, and by one estimate, lay a hundred fifty million eggs. But her story begins with one flight. A young queen leaves home with a tiny pellet of fungus in her mouth. That's her whole inheritance. She digs in, seals herself underground, and plants it. Only about two and a half percent build a colony that lasts. But the winners can end up with seven thousand rooms, more than twenty feet deep. So next time you see a leaf walking across the ground, remember where it's going. It's headed to a farm far older than us. Next up, another insect city, where workers talk by dancing. How does a honeybee hive work?

package.title: Why Does Popcorn Pop? 4x Your Car Tire's Pressure 🍿
package.description:
Why does popcorn pop? Water inside each kernel turns to steam, pressure builds to about 135 psi behind the hard hull, and at around 180°C it bursts and the starch puffs into foam up to 40 times bigger.

package.script: Your popcorn explodes at about 4 times, your car tire's pressure. Every kernel hides a bit of water, about 14 percent, packed in soft starch, locked inside a hard shell called the hull. Heat it up, and that water turns to steam. But the hull barely leaks, so steam has nowhere to go. Pressure climbs to about 135 pounds per square inch. Then, at around 180 degrees Celsius, the hull cracks. The starch blasts out and puffs into foam, up to 40 times bigger. And the pop you hear? That's not the shell breaking. It's the steam escaping. The first bit of starch forms a little leg, flinging the kernel into the air. Those duds in your bowl were too dry to build pressure. So, do you eat the ones that didn't explode?

Bursts at about 180°C
Can swell to 40-50 times its size (popcorn.org)
The pop sound comes from vapor release, not the hull cracking (Scientific American)
First starch forms a leg that catapults the kernel (popcorn.org)
Too-dry kernels don't build enough pressure

package.description:

package.script: Pineapple digests your tongue with every bite you take. That sting on your tongue, isn't just sour. Pineapple is packed with bromelain, a mix of enzymes that chop up protein. package.script: Your dog's wet nose traps smells you'll never notice, and it might even sense heat. That shine is a thin layer of mucus, made by tiny glands in the nose. Dogs have over a hundred million scent receptors. You've got about six million. But here's the strange part. topic.title: Why does hair turn grey?

package.title: Why Do 91% of Us Have Grey Hair by 65?
package.description:
Why does hair turn grey? Melanocyte stem cells in the hair follicle stop moving and get stuck, so fewer colour cells make melanin, a finding from a 2023 study in mice.

Sources:
https://www.livescience.com/health/ageing/why-does-hair-turn-gray
https://www.npr.org/2023/04/21/1171110131/gray-hair-stem-cells-reversible

Animated in the Napkin Sketch style.

package.pinned_comment: If scientists could unstick those cells, would you keep your grey or go back?
package.script: Your grey hairs start with stuck cells, tiny ones, at your roots. Hair gets its colour from melanin, a pigment made by cells called melanocytes. They sit at the bottom of each follicle, and inject colour as the hair grows. But those cells need replacing, and that's the job of stem cells. In mice, scientists found these stem cells commute, moving up and down the follicle. Moving is how they get the signal to make colour. But as hair ages, more of them stop. They get stuck in a spot called the bulge. In plucked mouse hair, stuck cells jumped, from fifteen percent to nearly fifty. Stuck cells can't make new colour cells. Less melanin means grey, no melanin means white. By your early sixties, about ninety-one percent of people have some grey. So if scientists could unstick those cells, would you keep your grey, or go back?
key_facts: Melanin made by melanocytes at the base of the follicle gives hair its colour (Live Science)
2023 Nature study: melanocyte stem cells migrate up and down the follicle in mice, and with age more get stuck, unable to mature (Live Science, NPR)

Less melanin gives grey hair, no melanin gives white (Live Science, citing the Library of Congress)

package.pinned_comment: Which hive job would you want: cleaner, nurse, builder, guard, or forager?
package.script: Sixty thousand bees, no boss, and you'd never guess how they run it. This hive builds perfect rooms, runs its own heating and cooling, and shares maps by dancing. So how does a honeybee hive actually work? Let's start with the queen. She sounds like the boss, but she doesn't give orders. Her real job is eggs. At her peak, she can lay up to fifteen hundred a day. That's about one egg every minute, all day and all night. Around her are a few hundred males, called drones. package.description:
Why do pigeons bob their heads when they walk? The head thrusts forward, then holds still in space while the body catches up, which keeps the bird's view of the world steady, and a 1978 treadmill experiment showed the bobbing stops when the surroundings don't move.

package.script: Pigeon heads never bob, you've been watching them freeze in midair. Watch one walk, the head shoots forward, about two inches. That's the thrust. Then it stops dead, locked in place, while the body walks underneath it. That's the hold. Then forward again, five to eight times every second. But why bother? In nineteen seventy-eight, scientists in Canada put a pigeon on a treadmill. Its legs kept walking, but the world around it stayed still, and the bobbing stopped. So it isn't about balance, it's about what the bird sees. Holding its head still keeps the view steady, like a camera on a tripod, while the world slides past. Chickens and cranes do it too. So next time you see a pigeon, watch the head. Is it bobbing, or standing still?

In 1978, researchers at Queen's University in Canada found the bobbing stopped when a pigeon walked on a treadmill with stationary surroundings, pointing to a visual response rather than balance (Live Science, Snopes).

package.pinned_comment: Which cheese has the best pull on your pizza?
package.script: Your pizza cheese hides a protein net, you've never seen. Long proteins called casein, are tied together by tiny calcium bonds, with fat and water stuck in the gaps. Cold, that net is stiff. Warm it up, and the fat melts first, then the bonds loosen. Now the strands slide past each other, without letting go. Mozzarella has an extra trick. Makers dunk the curd in hot water, around 70 to 80 degrees Celsius, then pull and fold it like dough, lining the proteins up in long fibers. Old cheese is different. As it ages, enzymes snip those strands, so it melts, but it won't stretch. Ricotta barely melts at all, its proteins are locked with permanent bonds. So a cheese pull is a net, bending but not breaking. Which cheese has the best pull on your pizza?

package.pinned_comment: Team fresh or team soap: what does cilantro taste like to you?
package.script: Your cilantro tastes like soap, to one in eight people, and you might be one. Same leaf, same taco. You get something fresh and lemony. Your friend gets a mouthful of dish soap. So who's right? Weirdly, you both are. And the answer starts in your nose. People have used this herb for thousands of years, all the way back to the Babylonians. And the haters have been loud. Before soap was the go-to insult, people said it smelled like bedbugs. Chef Julia Child once said, she'd pick it out of her food, and throw it on the floor. So how many people really dislike it? One Canadian study asked nearly fourteen hundred young adults. Dislike ran from just three percent, all the way up to twenty-one percent, depending on family background. And some of the lowest numbers came from people with Hispanic and South Asian roots, whose cooking uses cilantro all the time. Now, let's zoom in on one leaf. That smell is a big mix of chemicals, and some of the main ones are called aldehydes. Picture a long chain of carbon atoms, with one little oxygen on the end. One of them, called decenal, gets described as soapy, fatty and pungent. Here's the twist. Soap makers use aldehydes too. Cilantro and soap really do share a family of smells. Scientists still aren't sure which exact molecule is to blame. So why does only your friend notice? Scientists suspect this is mostly about smell, not taste. When you chew, scents float up the back of your throat, and into your nose. Up there, you've got hundreds of kinds of smell sensors. Think of them as tiny locks, and every scent molecule as a key. In twenty twelve, researchers at twenty-three and me, looked at the DNA of about twenty-five thousand people. They asked one question. Does cilantro taste like soap to you? And they found one tiny spot in the DNA, right next to a cluster of smell genes. One of those genes is called O R six A two, and it builds a lock that's great at catching aldehydes. Some people's noses may pick up that soapy note, a lot more loudly. Case closed, right? Not quite. Here's the number nobody expects. package.description:

package.pinned_comment: How many seconds can you go without blinking? Tell me your record!
package.script: You go blind fifteen thousand times every day. Why can't you tell? It's called blinking. Each blink lasts about a tenth of a second. The clear front of your eye has no blood vessels, so it relies on a film of tears instead. That film has three parts: mucus, water, and oil. Every blink wipes on a fresh coat, like a tiny windshield wiper, and sweeps dust toward your eye's drain. So why doesn't the world go black? Scientists scanned people's brains during blinks, and found parts of the visual system go quiet, right as your eyelid comes down. Your brain deletes the blackout, before you can ever see it. Altogether, your eyes are shut for about half an hour every day. So how many seconds can you go without blinking? Tell me your record.

Tear film spreads with each blink: mucus, water, oil; cornea has no direct blood supply

package.pinned_comment: What's your perfect toast: pale gold, or nearly burned?
package.script: You just ate molecules, your bread never had. That's what toast is. So why does it taste so much better? package.pinned_comment: If your tongue could smell, what would you follow first?
package.script: A snake's tongue can't taste a thing, so why do you see it flick nonstop? Because it's a scent collector. Each flick grabs tiny particles, from the air and the ground. The two tips spread apart, up to twice as wide as its head. So each tip samples a different spot, like your two ears. If the left tip smells stronger, dinner went left. That's smelling in stereo. In the air, the flicking tongue whips up tiny swirls, that pull smells in, sampling a hundred times more air, than a simple dip. If your tongue could smell, what would you follow first?

topic.title: Why do cows have a stomach with four compartments?

package.title: Why Do Cows Spend 8 Hours a Day Chewing Burps? 🐄
package.description:
Why do cows burp up their lunch and chew it again? A cow's one stomach has four compartments, and microbes in the giant rumen ferment tough grass that cows can't digest alone.

Sources:

package.pinned_comment: Would you chew your lunch twice, yes or no?
package.script: Cows burp up their lunch on purpose, and you'd never guess why. Grass is really hard to digest. Its walls are made of cellulose, and cows can't break that down alone. So one stomach has four rooms. Room one is the rumen, a vat holding up to forty gallons. It's packed with tiny microbes, and they ferment the grass. Room two, the honeycomb, sorts the pieces. Big chunks go back up her throat, as a soggy ball called cud. She chews it again, for about eight hours a day. Fine mush slides into room three, where water gets squeezed out. Room four is the true stomach, full of acid, like yours. All that fermenting makes gas, hundreds of litres of methane a day, and she burps it out. So, would you chew your lunch twice?
key_facts: One stomach with four compartments: rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum (MSU)
Rumen holds up to 40 gallons in a mature cow (MSU; other sources differ, hence 'up to')
Rumen microbes digest cellulose (MSU, Science Learning Hub)
Reticulum sorts small particles onward, larger stay for further digestion (MSU, Science Learning Hub)
Cows ruminate about a third of the day, ~8 hours (MSU; Purdue 35-40%)
Omasum absorbs water; abomasum is the true stomach with acid (all sources)
Cows burp 250-500 litres of methane a day (Science Learning Hub)

topic.title: How do dolphins sleep without drowning?

package.title: How Do Dolphins Sleep 8 Hours a Day Without Drowning?
package.description:
How do dolphins sleep without drowning when every breath is a choice? They rest one half of the brain at a time with one eye open, and in a 2012 test a dolphin stayed alert for 15 days straight.

Sources:
https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-do-whales-and-dolphin/
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/10/121017181244.htm
https://www.mpg.de/10673637/frigatebirds-sleep

Animated in the 16-Bit Pixel Odyssey style.

package.pinned_comment: If you could keep half your brain awake while the other half slept, what would you use the awake half for?
package.script: You sleep with your whole brain. Dolphins can't: one full nap and they'd drown. So how do they sleep eight hours a day? You pass out at night, and your body keeps breathing without asking. A dolphin doesn't get that deal. Dolphins are mammals, so they breathe air, like you. But every breath is a choice. The blowhole on top of its head is a flap of skin, and scientists think it opens on purpose, not automatically. The dolphin swims up, opens it, breathes out and in, then snaps it shut. So picture one falling fully asleep at sea. Nobody's at the controls. The air stops coming, and the water's right there. So how do you rest a brain that can never switch off? You switch off half of it. It's called unihemispheric sleep, which is a big word for one side at a time. One half of the brain drops into slow, deep waves. The other half stays awake, at low power, running the breathing, and watching for trouble. And you can actually see it from the outside. When the left half sleeps, the right eye closes. When the right half sleeps, the left eye closes. After about two hours, they swap. Each side gets roughly four hours across the day, so a dolphin sleeps about a third of its day, around eight hours. So what does that look like? Two moves. The first is called logging. The dolphin floats at the surface, barely moving, looking exactly like a log. The second is slow swimming, in big circles. In one study of pool dolphins, most of them circled counterclockwise. Breathing slows down too, from around ten breaths a minute, to as few as three. And the open eye has a job. When two dolphins rest side by side, it's the eye that faces the partner. Now, you'd expect half asleep to mean half useless. Researchers tested that in twenty twelve. They had two dolphins spot targets with echolocation, continuously, day and night. Both kept going for five days, with no signs of getting tired. Then the female kept going, for fifteen days. Fifteen, with near-perfect accuracy. Nobody knows how much longer she could've gone, because the test just stopped. So scientists think this trick isn't only about breathing. It may be about staying alert, too. Then there are the newborns. A baby dolphin rests while its mother swims, getting towed along in her slipstream. She can't stop swimming for the first several weeks. One study said mothers and calves barely sleep for a month. Other researchers watched closely, and saw eyes closing during swim rest, so scientists are still arguing about that one. And dolphins aren't alone. Mallard ducks at the edge of a group, keep one eye open, pointed away from the others. Frigatebirds sleep while flying, on trips of up to ten days, averaging just forty-two minutes a day. Back on land, they sleep over twelve hours. So half a brain is a trick nature keeps reusing. One side rests, one side breathes, and nobody drowns. Next question: what actually happens when a jellyfish stings you? It has no brain at all, so who gives the order?
key_facts: Dolphins are conscious breathers; the blowhole flap is thought to open under voluntary control
Unihemispheric sleep: one hemisphere sleeps and the opposite eye closes; sides swap after about two hours
Bottlenose dolphins sleep about 33% of the day by EEG, about four hours per hemisphere
Resting breaths fall from 8-12 to 3-7 a minute
2012 PLOS ONE: two dolphins echolocated for 5 days with no fatigue; the female went 15 days with near-perfect accuracy
Newborn sleep is disputed (Lyamin 2005 vs Sekiguchi and Gnone 2006)
Frigatebirds sleep 42 minutes a day in flight, over 12 hours on land

package.pinned_comment: Which part of you loses signal first: your foot, your hand, or your arm?
package.script: Why does your foot lose signal when you sit on it? Most people blame blood flow, but scientists call that mostly a myth. The real culprit is a nerve. Think of it like a garden hose, carrying signals instead of water. Messages run from your foot to your brain. So you cross your legs. That pressure pinches the nerve, like stepping on the hose. Signals get blocked, or come through scrambled. Your brain hears almost nothing, so your foot goes numb. Then you stand up. The nerve starts working again, but it isn't smooth yet. Messy signals rush through, and your brain probably reads them as tiny prickles. Those are pins and needles, and they usually fade in minutes. So which part of you loses signal first: your foot, your hand, or your arm?
key_facts: Pressure on a nerve temporarily blocks or disturbs its signals (NTNU's Martin Syvertsen Mykland, Science Norway; UNC's Rebecca Traub, ScienceAlert)
Cut-off blood flow as the cause is called 'mostly a myth' (Science Norway), though sources note blood flow inside the nerve may play a part
The tingling comes as nerves regain function; the exact mechanism isn't fully understood (ScienceAlert, Science Norway)
Pins and needles are usually annoying for a few minutes (Mental Floss)

package.title: How Do Mosquitoes Find You in the Dark From 50 Meters? 🦟
package.description:
How do mosquitoes find you in the dark? They follow the carbon dioxide you breathe out, then your body odor, then the infrared heat from your skin.

Sources:
https://experts.caltech.edu/news/mosquitoes-use-smell-see-their-hosts-47338
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2024/08/240822181042.htm
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07848-5

package.pinned_comment: Do mosquitoes always pick you, or someone else in your house?
package.script: How does a mosquito find you in the pitch dark? Your breath. Only females hunt you, because they need blood to make eggs. Every time you breathe out, you leave a trail of carbon dioxide. Scientists think she can smell it from up to fifty meters away, about half a football field. She follows that invisible trail. Closer in, she picks up your body odor. In daylight, she'd spot you from about fifteen meters, but tonight, that's no help. So here's her secret weapon. Tiny pits on her antenna tips sense the infrared heat your skin gives off, from about seventy centimeters away. In one lab study, adding that heat doubled how hard mosquitoes searched. Breath, then smell, then heat. And she lands. So tell me: do mosquitoes always pick you, or someone else?
key_facts: Only female mosquitoes bite; they need blood to develop eggs (ScienceDaily 2024, Caltech 2015).
Researchers hypothesize mosquitoes smell a CO2 plume from 10 to 50 meters (Caltech 2015, model-based).
They begin to see a host within 5 to 15 meters (Caltech 2015).
Aedes aegypti detect thermal infrared up to about 70 cm via antenna-tip peg-in-pit structures (Nature 2024).
Adding skin-temperature infrared doubled host-seeking, only alongside CO2 and odor (Nature 2024).
